blocks.md:
Most failures are not bugs. A file may be missing; text may not be a number. A function that can fail in an expected way returns a **`Result`**:

```rust
enum Result<T, E> {
    Ok(T),
    Err(E),
}
```

`T` is the type of the value on success and `E` the type of the error. Like `Option`, `Result` is in the prelude, and the compiler will not let you use the `T` until you have dealt with the possibility of `Err`.

blocks.title: unwrap and expect
blocks.md:
When an error would mean a bug, or in quick prototypes and tests, two shortcuts turn an `Err` into a panic:

- `.unwrap()` returns the `Ok` value or panics with a generic message.
- `.expect("why this should work")` does the same with your message. Prefer `expect` in real code, and phrase the message as the reason you believe it cannot fail: `.expect("hello.txt should be included in this project")`. Future readers, including you, will thank you.

blocks.md: Propagating is so common that Rust has an operator for it. Put **`?`** after an expression that returns a `Result`: if it is `Ok(v)`, the expression evaluates to `v` and the function continues; if it is `Err(e)`, the function **returns `Err(e)` immediately**. blocks.explain: `?` chains: `File::open(...)?` gives a `File`, on which `read_to_string` is called, and its result is checked by the second `?`. The `Read` trait must be in scope to call `read_to_string` on a file.

blocks.title: ? also converts the error
blocks.md: When the error types differ, `?` calls `From::from` on the error to convert it into the function's error type. That is how one function can use `?` on a parse error and an I/O error and return a single error type of its own. You will build such a type below.

blocks.title: Where ? can be used
blocks.md: `?` returns early, so it can only be used in a function whose return type it can return into: `Result` (or `Option`, where `?` on `None` returns `None`). Using `?` in a function that returns `()` is a compile error. `main` may return `Result<(), E>`: if it returns `Err`, the program prints the error and exits with a non-zero status.

In `last_char_of_first_line`, `?` on the `Option` returned by `next()` returns `None` early for empty text. When `main` returns `Err`, Rust prints `Error:` and the error's debug form.

blocks.title: Your own error type
blocks.md:
A function that can fail in several ways should return an error type that names those ways. The idiomatic shape is an **enum** with one variant per cause, plus two trait implementations:

- `Display`, so the error can be shown to a user with `{}`;
- `From<OtherError>` for each underlying error, so `?` converts automatically.

Implementing `std::error::Error` too (an empty `impl` is enough) lets your type work with any code that accepts errors in general. Traits get their own lesson in chapter 10; here is the pattern to copy:

blocks.title: Box<dyn Error> for applications
A parser that explains its errors
blocks.goal: Build an error enum, make ? convert into it, and propagate errors through several functions.
blocks.behavior:
Parse lines like `"temp 21.5"` (a sensor name, a space, a reading).
- `pub enum ReadingError { Empty, NoValue(String), BadValue(std::num::ParseFloatError), OutOfRange(f64) }` (already defined).
- Implement `std::fmt::Display` for it: `"empty line"`, `"no value for <name>"`, `"bad value: <parse error>"`, `"out of range: <value>"`.
- Implement `From<std::num::ParseFloatError>` for `ReadingError` (producing `BadValue`).
- `pub fn parse_reading(line: &str) -> Result<(String, f64), ReadingError>`: trims the line; empty → `Empty`; no space → `NoValue(name)`; value not a float → `BadValue` (use `?`); value outside -50.0..=150.0 → `OutOfRange(v)`.
- `pub fn average(lines: &[&str]) -> Result<f64, ReadingError>`: the mean of all readings; the first error stops it and is returned. An empty list gives `Err(ReadingError::Empty)`.
hints: `impl fmt::Display for ReadingError { fn fmt(&self, f: &mut fmt::Formatter) -> fmt::Result { match self { ... => write!(f, "...") } } }`
`let v: f64 = value.trim().parse()?;` works once `From<ParseFloatError>` is implemented.
blocks.solution_explain: `?` on `parse()` converts the `ParseFloatError` into `ReadingError::BadValue` through the `From` implementation. `(-50.0..=150.0).contains(&v)` reads better than two comparisons. `average` gets early return on the first bad line for free from `?`.

questions.q: What does `?` do when applied to `Err(e)` inside a function returning `Result<T, MyError>`?
questions.explanation: It returns early, converting the error with `From`.

questions.q: Why does `fn main() { let n: i32 = "5".parse()?; }` not compile?
options: `main` returns `()`, so `?` has nothing to return an error into
questions.explanation: Declare `fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>` or handle the error.

questions.q: Which converts a `Result<T, ParseIntError>` into a `Result<T, String>`?
What does a good custom error type usually implement?
questions.explanation: Many errors wrap non-Copy data like Strings; `Copy` is not needed.

questions.q: When is `Box<dyn Error>` a good error type?
options: In a library whose callers need to match on each cause
In an application's main or a quick tool that only reports errors
questions.explanation: It accepts any error, at the cost of callers not knowing which kinds can occur.

points: `Result<T, E>` is `Ok(T)` or `Err(E)`; the compiler makes you handle the error before using the value.
`unwrap` and `expect` panic on `Err`; prefer `expect` with a message saying why it should not fail.
`?` returns the error early and converts it with `From`; it works in functions returning `Result` or `Option`.
Libraries: an error enum with `Display`, `Error` and `From`. Applications: `Box<dyn Error>` is often enough.

terms.def: The enum Ok(T) | Err(E) returned by operations that can fail in expected ways.
Unwraps an Ok (or Some) value, or returns the error (converted with From) from the current function.
Returning an error to the caller instead of handling it where it occurred.
A boxed value of any type implementing std::error::Error; a catch-all error type.
The conversion trait that ? uses to turn one error type into another.
